meta.title: High-Fidelity Low Earth Orbit Determination with Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machines
meta.authorsHtml: Fabian Dallinger<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>, Benedikt Aigner<sup>1</sup>, Thomas Andert<sup>1</sup>, Roger Förstner<sup>1</sup>

abstract: Accurate orbit determination in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) requires dynamic models that capture non-ideal perturbations such as Earth’s non-spherical gravity field, atmospheric drag, solar radiation pressure, and third-body effects. Classical Weighted Least Squares and Extended Kalman Filter approaches are well established, but they typically require a sufficiently accurate initial state to ensure convergence [1, 2]. Building on the Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machine (PIELM) formulations introduced by Scorsoglio et al. [3–5], this paper investigates PIELMs as an efficient alternative for LEO orbit determination that can be trained without requiring an a-priori state estimate by coupling measurement fitting with enforcement of the equations of motion. The physics loss extends beyond twobody motion by embedding a high-fidelity acceleration model including spherical-harmonic geopotential perturbations up to degree and order 70 × 70, a cannonball drag model, solar radiation pressure with eclipse handling, and point-mass third-body perturbations. Results on a representative ISS LEO arc show that the extended force model enables accurate trajectory reconstruction and supports cold-start orbit determination in high-fidelity LEO settings.

blocks.html: Orbit determination in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) is commonly addressed with Weighted Least Squares (WLS) and Kalman filtering techniques [1, 2], which typically depend on an initial orbit estimate for reliable convergence. Physics-informed machine learning [6] aims to estimate spacecraft trajectories from observations without requiring an a-priori state estimate for convergence while enforcing the underlying dynamics. In this work, the trajectory is represented by a Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machine (PIELM) [7]. The key idea is to use a singlehidden-layer network with fixed hidden parameters and to estimate only the output weights via least squares under data and physics constraints.

This approach follows the physics-informed orbit determination line of work by Scorsoglio et al. [3–5]. While those studies demonstrate the no-initial-guess advantage in keplerian or non-LEO regimes, they either focus on different dynamical environments or use reduced perturbation sets depending on the application [5]. Here, we specifically investigate the feasibility of enforcing a higher-fidelity LEO force model directly in the physics loss.

The main contribution of this paper is to extend the PIELM orbit determination formulation to a high-fidelity LEO setting by embedding a perturbation-rich acceleration model in the physics residual, including 70 × 70 geopotential, Harris-Priester atmospheric drag, solar radiation pressure (SRP) with eclipse handling, and third-body effects of all major bodies in the solar system. This enables a focused assessment of how the physics-informed ELM framework behaves when the enforced dynamics reflect the dominant non-ideal perturbations that drive practical LEO orbit determination [1, 8].

We define an orbit determination test case for the International Space Station using simulated ground-based tracking from four stations: Kourou (French Guiana), Santa Maria (Azores, Portugal), Weilheim (Germany), and New Norcia (Western Australia). Station positions and local topocentric frames are modeled using SPICE [14]. The observation set comprises range ρ, azimuth Az, and elevation El sampled every 10 s during visibility, defined by an elevation mask of 5◦≤El ≤90◦. Measurement errors are modeled as zero-mean, uncorrelated Gaussian noise with standard deviations of 20 m in range and 0.01◦in both azimuth and elevation [8] as depicted in Figure 1.

As reference (“truth”) data, we use publicly available ISS ephemerides generated by the ISS Trajectory Operations and Planning Officer (TOPO) team at NASA’s Johnson Space Center [15]. blocks.html: A high-fidelity dynamical model is fitted to the reference ephemeris over one orbit and subsequently resampled at 10 s. The model includes the Joint Gravity Model 3 (JGM-3) spherical harmonic field up to degree and order 70 × 70 [16], third-body perturbations from the Sun, Moon, and major planets, SRP, and atmospheric drag [1, 2]. Atmospheric density is represented by the Harris–Priester model [12], eclipse transitions are modeled using a smooth conical shadow function [1], and third-body positions are obtained from the JPL DE440 ephemerides [13]. Numerical propagation is performed using an explicit Runge–Kutta scheme of order 8(5, 3) [17]. The ISS physical properties are set to an effective cross-sectional area of 1518.4 m2 and a mass of 459417 kg. Drag and radiation pressure coefficients are fixed to CD = 2.21 and CR = 1.3. For learning-based estimation, the angular measurements are encoded using the sine–cosine representation proposed by Scorsoglio et al. [3–5] to obtain bounded targets in [−1, 1] and avoid 2π wrap-around discontinuities. Range is normalized by the semi-major axis a0 of the considered ISS orbit. The normalized measurement vector used for both WLS and the PIELM-based approach is

We compare the proposed PIELM-based estimator against a classical batch WLS solution. The objective is to assess whether the PIELM architecture remains effective when both the dynamical model and the measurement setup are upgraded to a high-fidelity, topocentric range–azimuth– elevation tracking scenario in LEO.

For the PIELM, we use Nn = 50 hidden neurons and enforce the dynamics at Nf = 2000 uniformly spaced collocation points. The input time is normalized to [−1, 1] and σ(·) = tanh(·) is used with fixed W ∈[−1, 1]; β is initialized uniformly randomly in [0, 1]. We set λ ≈300 (empirical tuning) and solve the nonlinear least-squares problem using SciPy’s Trust Region Reflective (TRF) algorithm. Unlike WLS, the PIELM does not require an initial state (r0, v0); training starts from random β. The same high-fidelity force model described in Section 3 is used for both the WLS batch propagation and the physics residual within the PIELM loss.

Figure 2 reports the absolute position error components in the ECI frame over one orbital period after determination. Both methods converge to a trajectory that closely matches the reference ephemeris over the considered arc.

blocks.html: In the high-fidelity (HF) setting, the WLS solution yields maximum absolute errors of about 19 m in x, 10 m in y, and 19 m in z at the end of the arc, while the PIELM shows larger end-of-arc peaks of about 74 m in x, 30 m in y, and 55 m in z. The corresponding initial errors are below about 11 m for PIELM and below about 4 m for WLS. Overall, these results indicate that the PIELM architecture can recover the ISS trajectory under high-fidelity LEO dynamics and topocentric tracking geometry without requiring an initial state estimate. The end-of-arc peaks are consistent with boundary effects from reduced measurement constraints near the arc edges. Notably, the WLS baseline depends on the chosen a-priori state and degrades sharply as the initial mismatch increases, whereas the PIELM is trained without requiring an a-priori state estimate for convergence. Quantitatively, the WLS mean absolute error (MAE) increases across all three dimensions from the few-meter level (0.25% −0.75% mismatch) to O(102) m at 1% and O(103) m at 2% mismatch (sweep not shown). The position errors can also be expressed in the radial– along-track–cross-track (RSW) frame. Figure 3 confirms the ECI trends in the RSW frame, with radial and alongtrack components of similar magnitude, reflecting coupled effects of drag and high-degree gravity in LEO.

blocks.caption: Absolute position errors in the RSW frame over a single-orbit ISS arc for WLS (dashed) and PIELM (solid) determination under the same high-fidelity force model.

blocks.html: Figure 4 shows similar measurement-space residuals for both methods: angular residuals are at the millidegree level (below the injected 0.01° noise), and range residuals remain in the few-meter regime. This indicates that under the present weighting and collocation setup, the PIELM fits the tracking data comparably to WLS. To assess force-model fidelity, Table 1 reports the MAE for PIELM and WLS under a HF model and a Keplerian low-fidelity (LF) model. While HF yields meter-level MAEs for both methods, the LF mismatch increases errors by several orders of magnitude in LEO, highlighting the need for high-fidelity dynamics. Notably, LF degrades WLS more strongly than PIELM, suggesting partial robustness to dynamics mismatch, since it is less tightly tied to the assumed dynamics through state propagation. Note that LF is a deliberately strong mismatch; assessing moderate, realistic mismatches (e.g., truncated geopotential or biased drag) is left for future work.

blocks.html: These experiments demonstrate that a PIELM can be trained with a high-fidelity LEO force model embedded directly in the physics residual, extending prior physics-informed OD work to perturbation-rich LEO dynamics [3– 5]. In a topocentric range–Az/El tracking scenario, the method yields meter-level reconstruction under the HF model and supports cold-start determination without an a-priori state estimate. Related work has also extended the PIELM framework beyond the scope considered here, including covariance estimation for PIELM, first introduced in [18] and further evaluated in [19], as well as autoencoder-based deep PIELM architectures [20]. Future work will target boundary-aware regularization, adaptive loss weighting and collocation strategies [21], and assess robustness under sparse tracking or graded force-model mismatch. Results are shown for a single ISS arc; extending to multiple arcs and realistic force/parameter mismatches is planned, and similar trends are expected across many LEO scenarios.

This section provides additional details on the configuration and runtime of the numerical experiments. For the full high-fidelity force model, the training time was approximately 1 min 46 s, measured on an Intel® Xeon® W-2245 CPU with 8 cores, 16 threads, and a clock speed of 3.90 GHz. No GPU was used for training. When the physics loss was reduced to a Keplerian two-body model, the training time decreased to approximately 4 s. The most computationally intensive component is the evaluation of the sphericalharmonic gravity field within the physics loss. Replacing the spherical-harmonic model with a simple Newtonian potential reduced the training time from approximately 1 min 46 s to 16 s keeping the other perturbation forces and using the same hyperparameter configuration. The computational cost also depends on the chosen network size and collocation density, with the runtime increasing approximately linearly with the number of collocation points and quadratically with the number of hidden neurons. In the considered experiments, Nn = 50 hidden neurons were sufficient to obtain good MAE performance, while the higher-fidelity force models required a larger number of collocation points, with Nf = 2000 providing a suitable configuration. For the Keplerian case, Nf = 50 collocation points were sufficient. In addition, a 1:1 weighting between the physics and data losses yielded improved performance for the Keplerian case, while the loss weighting had no noticeable influence on the training time. The fixed input weights and biases were initialized using a Gaussian distribution and subsequently normalized, consistent with the procedure described in Section 4. A fixed seed for the NumPy random number generator was used throughout all experiments to ensure reproducibility. Changing the random seed resulted in small variations in the overall performance. For most tested seeds, these variations had only a minor effect on the MAE; however, a more systematic analysis of the seed dependence and strategies for reducing it is left for future work.
